The riot package API

Source: vignettes/riot-api.qmd 
library(riot)

This vignette describes the public API of {riot} and the internal design of the package. It is aimed at developers who want to extend riot or reuse its internal machinery.

Public API

The public API is deliberately small: two exported functions.

read_bundle() — import bundles

read_bundle(file, reference_file = NULL, bundle_data = list()) reads a tractography file and returns a bundle (or a single streamline when the file contains exactly one tract).

b <- read_bundle(system.file("extdata", "UF_left.vtk", package = "riot"))
#> Number of data points: 38697
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> ✔ The bundle stored in '/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/riot/extdata/UF_left.vtk' has been successfully imported.
class(b)
#> [1] "fiber::bundle" "S7_object"

The supported extensions are declared by the internal supported_formats():

riot:::supported_formats()
#> [1] "vtk" "vtp" "fds" "tck" "trk" "trx" "fib" "dpy"

Dispatch is by file extension:

  • .vtk, .vtp, .fds — the C++ readers ReadVTK(), ReadVTP(), ReadFDS();
  • .tck — read_mrtrix();
  • .trk — read_trk();
  • .trx, .fib, .dpy — the DIPY Python bridge through reticulate.

For the DIPY-backed formats, read_bundle() requires a reference_file and initialises the Python bridge with the internal check_dipy() helper.

write_bundle() — export bundles

write_bundle(x, file, reference_file = NULL) writes a bundle (or a single streamline) to a file, invisibly returning x so it can be used in pipes. The target format is chosen from the file extension of file.

out <- tempfile(fileext = ".vtk")
write_bundle(b, out)
#> Number of streamlines: 2042
#> Number of arrays: 0
#> ✔ The bundle stored in `b` has been successfully exported to '/tmp/RtmpR5d5W2/file1bec4a0fa451.vtk'.

Internal functions

The internal (non-exported) API is what the C++ layer and the format readers are built on.

Conversion between bundle objects and the C++ flat list

The C++ functions do not know about S7 objects. They exchange data through a flat named list with the columns:

  • X, Y, Z — point coordinates;
  • PointId — 1-based position of the point within its streamline;
  • StreamlineId — 1-based identifier of the streamline.

Additional columns hold per-point scalar attributes. Columns named by streamline_cols are treated as per-streamline attributes instead.

Two internal functions convert between the two representations:

  • flat_list_to_bundle(lst, streamline_cols = character(0)) — converts the flat list returned by ReadVTK(), ReadVTP(), ReadFDS(), or the TCK/TRK readers into a streamline or bundle;
  • bundle_to_flat_list(x) — converts a bundle or streamline back into the flat list expected by WriteVTK(), WriteVTP(), and WriteFDS().
flat <- riot:::bundle_to_flat_list(b)
names(flat)[1:5]
#> [1] "X"            "Y"            "Z"            "PointId"      "StreamlineId"

The conversion is O(points) rather than O(streamlines × points): it uses split(seq_along(sid), sid) once to group point indices per streamline instead of scanning all points for each streamline. This matters for the TRK reader, which can process hundreds of thousands of points.

The MRtrix reader

read_mrtrix() handles .tck and .tsf files. It is split into:

  • read_header() — parses the text header and derives the data offset, endianness, and element size;
  • read_tck() — reads the binary track data, using NaN separators between streamlines and an Inf terminator at the end;
  • read_tsf() — reads track-scalar data, matching scalars to streamlines.

read_mrtrix() merges .tsf scalar columns into the tracks when the timestamps, streamline counts, and point counts match.

The TRK reader

read_trk() reads the binary TrackVis format. It uses read_fixed_char_binary() for null-terminated header strings and retrieve_trk_endianness() to detect big/little endian by checking the hdr_size field (1000 bytes) at offset 996. The bulk of the parsing happens in the C++ function ReadTRK(), which reads the whole file body in a single fread() call and pre-allocates the output vectors after a counting pass.

The C++ layer

Four C++ entry points are registered via cpp11 and re-exported as internal R functions in R/cpp11.R:

R function C++ function Purpose
ReadVTK(path) ReadVTK read legacy .vtk polydata
ReadVTP(path) ReadVTP read XML .vtp polydata
ReadFDS(path) ReadFDS read medInria .fds XML bundle
ReadTRK(...) ReadTRK read TrackVis .trk (fast path)
WriteVTK(flat, path) WriteVTK write legacy .vtk
WriteVTP(flat, path) WriteVTP write XML .vtp
WriteFDS(flat, path) WriteFDS write medInria .fds

The readers return the flat list described above; the writers accept it. The VTK classes come from the rvtk package, which supplies pre-compiled VTK headers and libraries at compile time.

The FDS reader/writer use the bundled TinyXML-2 parser (zlib license). The bundled copy is modified to avoid printf/stdout in compliance with the Writing R Extensions manual.

The DIPY Python bridge

The formats .trx, .fib, and .dpy are handled by DIPY through {reticulate}. The internal state is kept in two package-level globals (io_stateful_tractogram, io_streamline), lazily initialised by check_dipy(). Reticulate’s py_require("dipy") ensures that a Python environment with dipy is available, provisioning it automatically when needed (reticulate >= 1.41).

These code paths are skipped during coverage (# nocov start/end) because they require a Python environment.

Adding a new format

To add a new native format:

  1. Implement a reader that returns the flat list (columns X, Y, Z, PointId, StreamlineId, plus optional attribute columns) and, if writable, a writer that accepts it.
  2. Register the extension in supported_formats().
  3. Add a branch in read_bundle() (and write_bundle() for writers).
  4. Add tests in inst/tinytest/; the TRK and TCK test files show how to build minimal binary fixtures without external tools.

The flat-list contract is the seam that keeps new formats decoupled from the S7 data model: readers only need to produce the list, and flat_list_to_bundle() takes care of the rest.
